name: Michael Keroularios
otherNames: Michael Cerularius or Caerularius, the Latin forms in Cornelius Will's edition
Μιχαὴλ ὁ Κηρουλλάριος, the Greek form in Michael Psellos's funeral speech; Κηρουλάριος in the heading of his first letter
knownFor: Patriarch of Constantinople when Rome's envoys, led by Humbert of Silva Candida, excommunicated him in July 1054. His synod of bishops cursed their sentence and its makers. Under Isaac Komnenos he was sent into exile, and by Michael Psellos's account he died before his trial.
dates: Patriarch from 1043, the year Cornelius Will gives; Konstantinos Sathas gives 25 March, in a year the scan reads as 1945. Will ends his patriarchate in 1059; a note in R. W. Blackmore's English edition of Mouravieff says he "sat till 1058". Psellos, in his history, places his exile and death under Isaac Komnenos, whom Sathas has entering the city on 31 August 1057. No source used here gives his year of birth or the date of his death
place: Constantinople, where Sathas says he was born, and its great church, Hagia Sophia; a place of exile under Michael IV, apart from his brother, by Psellos; the island of Imbros, where Psellos says he was held; Madytos, on the coast of Thrace, where Psellos says his ship put in on the way to trial
tradition: The Byzantine Imperial Church (Macedonian Era); The Byzantine Church after the Schism

keyWorks.title: First letter to Peter, patriarch of Antioch
keyWorks.about: written soon after Pope Leo IX died in April 1054, Will notes. It tells of the envoys' coming and blames Argyrus, the duke of Italy, for the letters they brought. It then lists the Latin customs he held against them, from unleavened bread at Mass, fasting on Saturdays and shaven beards to the addition to the creed. Held in Greek, with Jean-Baptiste Cotelier's Latin as revised by Will

keyWorks.title: Second letter to Peter of Antioch
keyWorks.about: a shorter account of the same events. It says he would not meet the envoys, since he was sure they could not be moved and it was not right to speak with them without the other patriarchs. It says his synod cursed their writing on the emperor's order

keyWorks.title: Edict of his synod, July 1054
keyWorks.about: issued in his name. It says the envoys came on Argyrus's advice and were not sent by the pope, and it curses their paper and all who wrote it or advised it. Held in Greek and Latin in Will's edition

traces: His letters and his synod's edict are the Greek side's own account of 1054. Will, who printed both sides, says that in the letters he repeated the old charges against the Roman church and added new ones.
Peter of Antioch, answering him, urged peace where neither God nor the faith was at risk. The Latins are our brothers, Peter wrote, even if rustic ways or ignorance often lead them astray.
Psellos says he arranged the marriage of his niece, who later reigned as empress. Sathas names her Eudokia, wife of Constantine Doukas.
Psellos says his successor gave him first place even in death and honored him with yearly feasts. Sathas names the successor as Constantine Leichoudes.
remembered: Psellos's funeral speech tells his exile and death as a martyr's contest. Sathas says Psellos gave it after Isaac's death, probably at the urging of Constantine Doukas.
Jean-Baptiste Cotelier, whose text of the letters Will reprints, calls him the head of the Greek schismatics and a deadly enemy of the Latin church.
Baronius, in his Annals as quoted in Will's notes, judged the first letter's charges either wholly false or trifling.

Sathas calls him a strict keeper of the church's teaching and customs, but sharp, quick to anger and above all a dangerous stirrer of crowds. He says Michael broke Constantinople's ties with Rome for good.

uncertain: Most of his life is told by Michael Psellos, in a funeral speech of praise and in his history. Psellos served Isaac Komnenos, who sent him into exile, and Konstantinos Sathas says Psellos was forced to write the charge against him. The envoys' sentence of 1054 is a hostile witness.

His death. Psellos says that at Madytos the dead bishop Euthymios told him in a dream that his crown was ready. He then crossed toward the court in Thrace, foretold his death and died before the trial, forgiving the emperor, his judges and all who had wronged him. Sathas says instead that he heard the charge in silence before the court, forgave his judges and the emperor, and fell dead. Psellos's history says the news reached Isaac from far off, and that he cried out and repented. Sathas says Isaac threw himself on the body.

His part in the revolt of 1057. Psellos says he calmed the crowds in Hagia Sophia and, when Michael VI's throne was lost, took in the emperor and embraced him in tears. Sathas says he armed the crowds and the clergy, declared the emperor deposed and then sheltered him.
Where he was held. Psellos names the island of Imbros, and so does Sathas. Sathas adds that Skylitzes says he was taken to Prokonnesos. No text of Skylitzes is among the sources used here.

The end of his patriarchate. Will gives 1059, and Blackmore's note to Mouravieff says he "sat till 1058". For the start, Will and Blackmore give 1043; Sathas gives 25 March, in a year the scan reads as 1945.

Why he and the envoys never met. The envoys' account says he avoided them. In his first letter he says they would not greet him, bow, or sit below his metropolitans. In his second he says he himself declined to talk with them.
The day his synod cursed the envoys. The edict as Will prints it gives 20 July; Will notes that copies read the twenty-fourth, and corrects them. Sathas gives 24 July.

The plot under Michael IV. Psellos says the plotters chose him without his knowledge, and that all of them called him innocent. Sathas dates the plot to 1040 and says he was forced into the monk's habit.
Psellos at the synod of 1054. The emperor's letter to the synod came by three men, among them Constas, vestarch and head of the philosophers. Sathas takes Constas to be Psellos.

The charge at his trial. Sathas says Psellos accused him of backing two monks of Chios and a woman who gave oracles, of alchemy, and of stirring the revolt against Michael VI. Psellos's charge is not among the sources used here.

His dress and words before the arrest. Sathas says he wore an emperor's red sandals and threatened Isaac with a common saying: I built you, oven, and I will pull you down. No line of Psellos held here says this; Sathas's note for the passage cites Psellos, the charge, Skylitzes and Attaleiates.
